claims.text: Mechanical disruption of the passive film at the sliding interface is the dominant factor governing tribo-corrosion in high-entropy alloys.
Mechanical passive-film disruption causes localized depassivation and exposes fresh alloy to the corrosive medium.
The proposed alloy initially has an established passive surface layer under moderately corrosive conditions.
Varying normal load and electrochemical potential while holding sliding speed and solution chemistry constant can isolate their effects on tribo-corrosion.
Higher contact loads increase the rate and frequency of passive-film removal.
Certain applied electrochemical potentials increase the rate and frequency of passive-film removal.
More frequent film removal slows effective repassivation.
Continued mechanical damage permits more aggressive corrosion.
The coupled process produces total material loss greater than the additive losses from wear and corrosion acting separately.
Increasing normal load will cause total degradation to rise faster than the sum of purely mechanical wear and pure corrosion.
Applying a more oxidizing potential will cause total degradation to rise faster than the sum of purely mechanical wear and pure corrosion.
Synergy-driven damage may contribute on the order of tens of percent of total degradation.
A prior report attributed approximately half of total mass loss to erosion-corrosion synergy.
Low-load tests with minimal passive-film damage and near-neutral potential will exhibit minimal synergistic degradation.
If a stable passive film cannot form, film rupture will make a diminished contribution to tribo-corrosion.
The predicted load and potential trends may fail at extremely low pH or in alloys with poor film-forming ability.
A lack of significant change in synergistic mass loss when load or potential is varied would falsify the claim that mechanical film disruption governs the synergy.
